headline: Heathrow and Rosebank Disputes Threaten Burnham’s Labour Unity
author: Lucy White

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 27, 2026 at 6:49 AM EST 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Controversial decisions over a North Sea oil field and one of the world's biggest airports are threatening to shake the unity that Prime Minister Andy Burnham has brought to Britain's ruling Labour Party.

Almost 100 Labour Members of Parliament have written to the government to express concerns about the possibility that it will approve development of the Rosebank oil field — just weeks after it angered some left-wing colleagues by giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field. The letter includes four signatories from Labour's front benches, the Guardian newspaper reported.

A critical report from Parliament's Transport Select Committee on Thursday also lambasted the government for failing to "make the case" for a third runway at London's Heathrow Airport. The much-delayed project is set to deepen divides between Labour MPs who think it would help boost growth, and those who are concerned about the impact on carbon emissions and noise levels.

The contentious issues present a dilemma for Burnham, who has been credited with smoothing over rifts in the party following his appointment as premier in July. One MP said that Burnham has kept in contact with MPs and focused on more left-wing issues such as the cost of living, bringing a sense of calm to a party that had become increasingly disgruntled and fractious under his predecessor Keir Starmer — however, they warned that such tactics wouldn't necessarily be enough to maintain unity on divisive issues such as Rosebank.

In an article written for the Guardian, Labour MP Catherine Fookes — who organized the protest letter — said that "if Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil giants." She added that it would "not make an iota of difference to our constituents' energy bills" and would "accelerate the climate crisis."

Meanwhile the Transport Committee — chaired by Labour's Ruth Cadbury — said in a 96-page report on Thursday that plans for the £33 billion ($43 billion) Heathrow expansion were not compatible with climate goals and would bring only a "modest" level of economic growth.

The committee urged the government to improve its case for the runway, strengthening the air quality and noise tests, and said more detail should be provided over the cost of the expansion and plans to increase public transport to the airport.
